unlock.arabic_transcription: فاما الاموال والجذور التي تعدل العدد فمثل قولك مال وعشرة اجذاره يعدل تسعة وثلثين درهما ومعناه اي مال اذا زدت عليه مثل عشرة اجذار بلغ ذلك كله تسعة وثلثين ـ فقياسه ان تنصف الاجذار وهي في هذه المسئلة خمسة فتضربها في مثلها فيكون خمسة وعشرين فتزيدها علي التسعة والثلثين فيكون اربعة وستين فتاخذ جذره وهو ثمانية فتنقص منه نصف الاجذار وهو خمسة فيبقي ثلثة وهو جذر المال الذي تريد والمال تسعة
unlock.our_translation: As for the squares and the roots which equal a number: it is like your saying, “a square and ten of its roots equal thirty-nine dirhams” — its meaning being, which square is it that, when you add to it ten of its roots, the whole amounts to thirty-nine? The rule for it is that you halve the roots, which in this problem is five, and you multiply it by itself, and it becomes twenty-five; you add it to the thirty-nine, and it becomes sixty-four; you take its root, which is eight, and you subtract from it half the roots, which is five, and three remains — and that is the root of the square you wanted, and the square is nine.

critic._note: The benchmark. The similarity score is computed IN CODE at runtime from these two strings (code-spine §2.3). The model never reports its own confidence.
critic.benchmark_text: Roots and Squares are equal to Numbers; for instance, “one square, and ten roots of the same, amount to thirty-nine dirhems;” that is to say, what must be the square which, when increased by ten of its own roots, amounts to thirty-nine? The solution is this: you halve the number of the roots, which in the present instance yields five. This you multiply by itself; the product is twenty-five. Add this to thirty-nine; the sum is sixty-four. Now take the root of this, which is eight, and subtract from it half the number of the roots, which is five; the remainder is three. This is the root of the square which you sought for; the square itself is nine.

lineage.contribution: Wrote the first systematic treatise on solving equations by balancing (al-jabr). The book’s title gave us the word algebra; his own name, Latinised as algorismus, gave us algorithm.
lineage.how_they_thought: He refused to treat each equation as its own puzzle. Instead he sorted every quadratic into six canonical types, and wrote one repeatable procedure for each — then proved each procedure geometrically, so the rule was not merely asserted but seen. The move is: reduce the unfamiliar to a known shape, then apply the stored method.

algorithm._note: The universal layer — present for every objective regardless of lineage tier.
algorithm.name: Reduce to a known shape
steps: Look at what you have: x² + 10x. It is not a square — it is a square with a strip attached.
Halve the roots. Ten roots become two strips of five.
Move the strips to two sides of the square. Now you have an L-shape.
See what is missing: one corner, five by five — twenty-five.
Add it to BOTH sides. The shape is now a true square; the equation is still balanced.
Read off the side, then undo the shift.
socratic_prompts: You have a square and ten strips laid beside it. What shape is it closest to?
If you had to split the ten strips to keep the shape symmetrical, how would you split them?
Look at the corner. What exactly is missing — and what is it worth?
You added twenty-five to one side. What does fairness demand you do to the other?

apply.problem: Solve x² + 6x + 5 = 0 by completing the square.
apply.hint: Six roots. How do you split them so the shape stays symmetrical?
reveal_steps: Half of 6 is 3, so the bracket is (x + 3).
(x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9 — but we only had 5, not 9.
The bracket added 9. We had 5. So we must take away 4: (x + 3)² − 4.
That −4 is the overlap — the corner we borrowed but did not own.
apply.mark_scheme: M1 for (x + 3)². A1 for −4. A1 for both roots. Full marks require the completed square form to be shown, not just the roots.

story.title: al-jabr
the_word: The book is called Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala — the Compendious Book on Calculation by Restoration and Balancing.
al-jabr — restoration. You have something subtracted on one side; you restore it by adding it to both. The negative goes away.
al-muqābala — balancing. Whatever is the same on both sides, cancel it. What is left is simpler and still true.
Those two moves are the whole of school algebra. You have been doing al-jabr since you were eleven and nobody told you its name.
The word travelled: al-jabr → algebra. And the author's own name, al-Khwārizmī, Latinised as algorismus, became algorithm.

why_he_wrote_it.lead: Not for mathematicians. He says so himself, in the opening pages:
why_he_wrote_it.quote: …confining it to what is easiest and most useful in arithmetic, such as men constantly require in cases of inheritance, legacies, partition, law-suits, and trade, and in all their dealings with one another, or where the measuring of lands, the digging of canals, geometrical computation, and other objects of various sorts and kinds are concerned.
why_he_wrote_it.after: Inheritance disputes. Land boundaries. Trade. Canals. This was written to settle arguments about real money and real ground — and the algebra your exam asks for was invented as a tool for that job.

where_now: A ball thrown in the air
Its height is a quadratic in time. Complete the square and the answer falls out: the highest point it reaches, and exactly when.
Anything you want the most or least of
Maximum area from a fixed fence, maximum profit, minimum cost. Same move every time.
Complete the square twice — once in x, once in y — and the centre and radius appear.
The formula is not a separate thing to memorise. It is completing the square, done once, in general, for every quadratic at once. You have been using his method all along.

suggested: Why does completing the square actually work?
Where would I ever use this?
What if b is an odd number?
Is this the same as the quadratic formula?

qa.answer: Because a square is a shape you can complete. x² + bx is a square with a strip stuck to one side. Halve the strip, move the halves to two sides, and there is exactly one corner missing — (b/2)². Add it, and you have a true square. You add it to both sides, so the equation stays true. That is al-jabr: restoring the balance.

Anywhere something has a maximum or a minimum. The height of a thrown ball, the biggest area you can fence, the lowest cost. Completing the square turns the expression into (x + a)² + b, and that b is the answer — because a square is never negative, the smallest the whole thing can ever be is b. al-Khwārizmī used it for inheritance shares and land measurement.

Nothing breaks. Halving an odd number gives a fraction, and the method carries on unchanged. For x² + 5x, half of 5 is 2.5, so the bracket is (x + 2.5)² and you subtract 2.5² = 6.25. Cambridge will often accept the fraction form — (x + 5/2)² − 25/4 — which is tidier than decimals.

al-jabr means restoration. If you have x² − 4x = 5, the −4x is a deficiency; you restore it by adding 4x to both sides. Its partner al-muqābala means balancing — cancelling what is identical on both sides. Those two words are the title of the book, and al-jabr became the word algebra.

It is the same thing. Take ax² + bx + c = 0 and complete the square using letters instead of numbers, and what drops out is x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. The formula is his method done once, in general, so nobody has to redo it. When you use the formula you are running al-Khwārizmī's procedure without noticing.

He did not have algebraic notation — that came centuries later. So he proved it by drawing: an actual square of side x, with rectangles laid along two edges, and a corner missing. The proof is visible rather than symbolic, which is why the diagram in this lesson is his and not a modern illustration.
